newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: SHORT TERM STILL LOOKING BLEAK FOR MANUFACTURERS
The Federal Government is being called on to show its commitment to manufacturing by reversing cuts to research and development programmes, and pressuring the Reserve Bank to cut interest rates.
The Australian Chamber of Manufacturers' Executive Director, Allan Handberg, says big spending cuts in last year's budget didn't help the jobs situation in the short term.
Mr Handberg says he's hoping Government reforms will lead to an economic upswing, and growth in investment, which will in turn boostjobs.
But he says it's worrying that the Government doesn't expect this to happen in the next six months.
COSTELLO SIGNALS FURTHER SPENDING CUTS
The Coalition Government's commitment to honour a tax cut promise made by the former Labor Government appears to be wavering.
The Keating Government promised four-billion dollars worth of tax cuts, which were later transformed into superannuation contributions.
But although the Coalition promised to deliver on Mr Keating's promise, Treasurer, Peter Costello, now says he can't rule the cuts in or out.
The Government says the four billion dollars has been budgeted for, but ways of distributing the money are under review.
Mr Costello is also promising a further crackdown on tax avoidance in this year's budget, as a way of hauling in a three billion dollar deficit blowout.
Mr Costello's second budget will also contain further spending cuts, but they won't be as austere as as last year's, and won't undermine the social security safety net.
Some budget measures rejected last year are also set to be returned to the Senate.
GOOD NEWS ON INFLATION EXPECTED
Economists are expecting excellent news on inflation when the latest CPI figures are released today.
Inflation for the December quarter is tipped to rise by between point-one and point-five of one percent.
Economists say this would be in line with the Government's improved inflation outlook, announced in its budget review yesterday.
ANZ Group Chief Economist, Saul Eslake, says an increase in the headline rate of point-one of one per cent would cut the annual inflation rate from 2.1 percent percent to 1.4 percent.
Mr Eslake says the underlying inflation rate should fall from 2.4 percent to two percent.
It's predicted that a fall in housing-related prices, reflecting recent cuts to mortgage interest rates, should counter price rises for food, transport and health-care in the December quarter.
Mr Eslake says the Reserve Bank will be closely watching both the underlying and headline inflation trends to decide whether the economy can cope with another interest rate cut.
MURDER MYSTERY SPANS THE GLOBE
An investigation into a bizarre murder in Britain has led to a hunt for a couple in Western Australia.
The body of 58-year-old art teacher, Janice Crompton, was found wrapped in plastic inside a pick-up truck in North Devon last week.
Mrs Crompton had suffered a fractured skull, and a hive of bees was found on top of her body.
The body was found in a truck belonging to a friend of Mrs Crompton, Clifford Harris, who is believed to be touring Australia with his wife Margaret.
British police have described the case as a real mystery and have assigned 50 officers to the investigation.
Interpol and the Australian Federal Police believe Mr and Mrs Harris were due to travel to Perth, before flying to South Australia to visit their son Phillip, who lives in Adelaide.
HOWARD JOINS HAWKE AND KEATING IN BALLARAT PARK
Prime Minister John Howard is in Ballarat today to unveil a bronze bust of himself.
The bust is the latest addition to Prime Ministers' Avenue in Ballarat's botanic gardens.
The bust's sculptor, Peter Nicholson, has also immortalised prime ministers Fraser, Hawke and Keating for the avenue.
Mr Howard will also launch a 250-thousand dollar appeal for the Lake Wendouree Museum and officially open multi-million dollar extensions to Ballarat's School of Mines.
NATIVE TITLE LINKED TO HEALTH OF ABORIGINES
Labor's Aboriginal Affairs spokesman, Daryl Melham, says failure to secure native title could have a detrimental impact on the health of Aboriginal people.
Mr Melham and Shadow Health Minister, Michael Lee, are visiting Aboriginal-run health groups in Alice Springs.
Mr Melham says the visit has confirmed his view that the debate about native title in the wake of the High Court's Wik decision has much wider implications than most people realise.
He says secure title to land can dramatically improve the psychological and physical well-being of indigenous people.
